title: Change Healthcare is a Big Enough Problem for United Healthcare to Notice.
subtitle: Optum lays off security team...in the middle of a ransomware attack?
text:
The Frontier Psychiatrists is thrilled to bring you the late-breaking news in the ongoing Change Healthcare—BUT IN WHICH DIRECTION?—saga. This article has a pay wall, there is original reporting therein, and it's a whole to do.

In our prior installment, we covered the fact that Change Healthcare—acquired by UnitedHealthgroups’s Optum Sub-division—had a cyber attack that led to an SEC filing about the attack being ransomware. This is sort of hilarious, because if anyone is holding American health data hostage…it’s American healthcare. Remember when I wrote joke press releases about Leviathan Eating All That Is? Or made fun of the earnings call a biblical world-ending monster would have? Feels a bit…to close to reality now.

Subscribe now

We have breaking updates, and, in a surprising turn of events, some original reporting on this story!

It turns out it’s not a state actor, per se, it’s the Ransomware crime syndicate called “BlackCat”—which is an adorable name for a cybercrime ring. BlackCat is RaaS— criminal, but they are a “ransomware as a service” group. A criminal enterprise, that sells its ransomware software, for a price and a portion of the proceeds. Everybody's a platform now?

This is a bad problem, and getting more grim by the day given the group involved: (from HIPAA Journal)

On February 27, 2024, a member of the Blakcat group confirmed that they were behind the attack.

Blackcat is known to engage in double extortion tactics, where sensitive data is exfiltrated before ransomware is used to encrypt files. Ransoms must be paid to recover encrypted files and to prevent the release of stolen data, so there is likely to have been a data breach although that has not been confirmed by Change Healthcare at this stage

It is also absurd, but true, that in the middle of a massive cyberattack the scale of which has shut down access to lifesaving drugs, at, for example, ALL MILITARY PHARMACIES, Optum was busy laying off much of its cybersecurity team.

From thelayoff.com:

Granted, these are anonymous internet comments, let’s take them with a grain of salt.

it also seems like the US Department of Justice is taking a very serious look at United Healthcare: The examiner reports…

significant local layoffs were enacted last week.

…UnitedHealth Group, Optum’s publicly traded corporate parent, received notice on Oct. 10, 2023, that the Department of Justice (DOJ) had launched a “non-public antitrust investigation into the company,” according to a message distributed on Oct. 24 by Rupert Bondy, an executive vice president and chief legal officer of UnitedHealth Group.

Bondy’s e-mail, sent to high-ranking colleagues, concedes the disconcerting and potentially significant nature of the executives receiving a “document preservation notice” from federal law enforcement, acknowledging the “breadth of the notice” issued by U.S. authorities.

The legal tactic of service for preservation of records means don't destroy anything. That we're gonna look, and then we need all the records there. This is a big deal. A very big deal. This is not the Federal Trade Commission. This is the Department of Justice. The Department of Justice can put you in jail. I think that's highly unlikely…but anti-trust enforcement, especially in the context of a very high-profile ransomware attack, where the FBI could be of help in decrypting files…

We have an adverse outcome of a very monopoly-ish company. We have millions of patient records at risk. We had terrible decision-making around staffing of cyber security infrastructure and team members right before a major high-impact breach that impacted military pharmacies. This is a huge problem. And with a pre-existing preservation of records order from earlier last year, it's terrible timing for the UnitedHealth group at a minimum.

The firings have been massive, enough to trigger a local labor law called WARN—where major companies with layoffs greater than 50 are supposed to provide 90 days prior notice.

And, guess what day they started? That's right, the two days before the cyber security crisis…was reported on the 21st. The layoffs included both cyber security professionals and those who would be impacted by the subsequent breach as providers and, other cogs in the machine like the people who do prior authorization for the provider side of Optum, to deal with the prior authorization requirements on the United healthcare side of Optum:

My local doctor source confirmed that 28 pre-certification representatives were let go last week, some by e-mail, some by a phone call.

“It’s happening two weeks before they get their yearly bonus, and their yearly meeting to increase their hourly wage,” the doctor told me through an intermediary.

So here's the fun and original reporting part of this article: I spoke to a cybersecurity professional. It was on background. I'll present, unattributed, what I was told…

The average time between accessing a network like Change Healthcare and discovering that the network had been penetrated is on the order of 204 days. It is then an average of 73 days until the breach is sealed off. It is rumored, although not confirmed, that there has been a breach utilizing a ChangeWise exploit, which is previously known. ChangeWise is an IT platform that had a security breach, that let hackers get into the Change Healthcare system, but they just kind of hang out and collect data while they're there. And 1/3 of America's healthcare was being collected, logins, multifactor authentication, etc. we're being collected to allow direct access to the healthcare infrastructure for our ransom criminals.

The average, as I mentioned, is 73 days until these ransomware attacks are resolved, but we're not dealing with reliable actors—just because you buy the decrypt key for your data, doesn't mean they're not gonna hit you the very next day all over again by re-encrypting it. It's hard to deal with unreliable criminals reliably. Change Healthcare may be down for a very long time. The market rate for a breach of the scale is around $40 million, which is not that much money for United Healthcare, which made $8.9 billion last quarter. However, that $40 million would go to terrorism or crime or more of this nonsense. The FBI’s advice is don't pay ransom. The advice of the IRS as you can write off the losses from paying off the ransom. This seems like contradictory advice.

The much bigger financial problem for United Healthcare is that the information in question is all protected health information, that, for an average of hundreds of days, was being accessed by somebody in a way that is a violation of HIPAA. Keep in mind, they just laid off a significant number of cybersecurity professionals, in an industry where there are 800,000 open cybersecurity jobs currently. These are hard-to-hire individuals, and somewhat dangerous to fire, frankly.

We know the date on which they reported the HIPAA breach to the Securities and Exchange Commission, but they had 48 hours to do that (actually to HHS, and we don’t know when it did that). If there is documentation that they knew before, the fines on the HIPAA breach and the scale of that HIPAA breach may be financially catastrophic in a way that a $40 million ransom payment would be trivial next to.

“What did they know and when did they know it” is going to be a really important question. And given the fact that they just fired a bunch of people, there may be some pissed-off for our cyber security professionals who have every incentive to report what they knew. Remember that preservation records request from the DOJ?

Keep in mind, that the actual security standards in the field, which determine whether the insurance that United Healthcare has taken out to cover cybersecurity breaches will cover it, state you're supposed to have an “air gap” on your data. That means you're supposed to have all of the data that could be ransomed backed up—on computers that are not connected to the main Internet that can be invaded.

And my guess is they were out of compliance with that cyber security standard. The cyber security issue is the least of United Healthcare's problems, it's the HIPAA breach on top of the cyber security invasion that causes a compliance nightmare the scale of which, I hope to illustrate appropriately.

Here is what those HIPAA breaches can cost: keep in mind this is per patient record…

A tier 4 breach, if there is willful neglect found, and not corrected within 30 days, 1.8 million maximum per patient record. Keep in mind, that Change Healthcare processes data on 1/3 of Americans. That's 100 million people. So we're talking about a worst-case scenario of $1.8×10^14. I don't think I have to point out that when you have to go into scientific notation, it's a big fine. It's 377 times bigger than the market capitalization of UnitedHealth Group today.

That's a worst-case scenario. But it is so bad that it's important to a company like United Healthcare. It is orders of magnitude bigger than their market capitalization, which is the largest healthcare company on earth, and is a big deal.

It’s also a big deal to all of us, out here, not getting paid, not getting our meds, not getting our healthcare to you know, work. All of us should care. And will, in the coming days.

All of this may explain why the Department of Justice is interested in the following (per the WSJ):

"During their interviews, investigators have asked about issues including certain relationships between the company’s UnitedHealthcare insurance unit and its Optum health-services-arm, which owns physician groups, among other assets.”

"Investigators have asked about possible impacts of the company’s doctor-group acquisitions on rivals and consumers [and] have also explored whether Optum’s ownership of healthcare providers could present challenges to health insurers that are rivals to UnitedHealthcare."

I'm not saying she's a gold digger, but the DOJ ain’t investigating no broke players in US healthcare for antitrust violations.
